title: Senate Bill Asks Labor Department for a Plan on PERM Premium Processing
excerpt: Appropriators want a report within 60 days of enactment on a fee-based fast track for green card labor certifications that now average about 300 days — but no premium option exists yet.
body:
• A Senate spending bill's explanatory statement, released November 16, directs the Department of Labor to report within 60 days of enactment on speeding up PERM labor certifications, including “launching a fee-based premium processing option.”
  • Nothing is available today: employers cannot pay to expedite a PERM case, the Labor Department charges no filing fee for Form ETA-9089, and report language in an explanatory statement does not by itself create a programme.
  • The wait it targets is long — PERM cases decided in the 30 days before October 31, 2026 averaged about 300 days at analyst review, according to the Labor Department's Office of Foreign Labor Certification.
  • A separate House bill, the PERM Backlog Reduction Act (H.R. 10051), would create the fast track directly: an optional $1,200 fee for 30-day processing of Form ETA-9089.

The Senate has formally asked the Department of Labor to explain how it could offer premium processing for PERM labor certifications — the paid fast track that employment-based green card sponsorship has never had. The explanatory statement for the fiscal 2027 Labor-HHS spending bill, released by the Senate Appropriations Committee on November 16, directs the department to report within 60 days of the bill's enactment on its efforts to speed up PERM cases, including “launching a fee-based premium processing option,” according to a detailed analysis of the statement by Immigration Analytics.

Who this affects — and who it does not

PERM is the Labor Department's permanent labor certification: before an employer can sponsor a worker for an EB-2 or EB-3 green card, it must usually complete PERM, which includes testing the US labor market through recruitment and filing Form ETA-9089. The workers behind those filings are disproportionately H-1B professionals — many of them Indian nationals — for whom a filed PERM also underpins extensions of H-1B status beyond six years. The Senate language concerns only this Labor Department stage. Counted here: DOL's handling of the labor certification itself. Not counted: the USCIS I-140 petition that follows, Visa Bulletin priority-date waits, or adjustment of status — a faster PERM would shorten one stage of the green card process, not the whole timeline.

What the Senate is asking for

Under the heading “Timely Processing of Permanent Labor Certification Applications,” the committee tells the department to use its existing authority and resources to improve processing timelines so employers have more certainty. The 60-day report must cover four things: steps to shorten PERM processing; expanding concurrent processing between the department's labor certification work and DHS visa processing; launching an optional, fee-based premium processing fast track; and closer security coordination between the Labor Department and DHS. The same statement provides $63,528,000 for foreign labor certification activities.

Why a report is not yet a fast lane

The mechanism matters. PERM works like this: the employer recruits, files Form ETA-9089, and waits for an analyst decision — a wait that the Office of Foreign Labor Certification puts at an average of about 300 calendar days for cases decided in the 30 days before October 31, 2026, and 360 days measured over the prior 180 days. Unlike USCIS, which has long offered premium processing for I-140 and I-129 petitions, the Labor Department charges no PERM filing fee at all today, so there is no fee structure to bolt a fast track onto. And explanatory-statement language is not statute: agencies usually respond because appropriators control their budgets, but the language alone does not give the department authority to collect and spend a new fee. Whether DOL could build a paid track on its own authority is the open question the report would have to answer.

The legislative route already in the House

A direct route exists in the House. The PERM Backlog Reduction Act (H.R. 10051), introduced by Rep. Glenn Grothman, R-Wis., and Rep. Lou Correa, D-Calif., would create an optional $1,200 fee for 30-day processing of Form ETA-9089, with fees funding staffing, training, adjudication, system upgrades and fraud detection, and a requirement that the premium track not slow standard processing, Assembly Magazine reported. The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee; Grothman's office has published an announcement of the proposal.

What to do next

For employers and workers with a PERM case pending or planned, the correct action today is nothing new: there is no premium option to buy, and no fee to budget until one of these routes becomes law and the Labor Department implements it. The two dates to watch are enactment of the fiscal 2027 Labor-HHS bill — which starts the 60-day clock for DOL's report — and any movement of H.R. 10051 out of committee. The Senate push lands as the department separately rewrites PERM's rules: our earlier coverage explains the proposed PERM overhaul, which would lengthen recruitment and restrict filings by employers with recent layoffs.
